catalog_quote: Wondwosen (2015) uses the term tone-accent to describe Mositacha. By this, he means that each lexical word has only one high tone per word. According to his analysis, there are two tones – high and low – but he says that these tones are not contrastive as they do not carry meaning. Exactly what he means by this is unclear, but he may be referring to an absence of minimal pairs differentiated only by tone. I respectfully disagree with Wondwosen’s terminology and analysis that tone is not phonemic. Additionally, Wondwosen’s description states that tone in Mositacha is culminative; that is, a lexical word can have at most one prominent syllable; however, tone does not seem to be obligatory. As we will see, some lexical words do not have a syllable that is more prominent than the others. [...] Among disyllabic and trisyllabic nouns, there are three main pitch patterns found: HL, LH, and level. Because the dataset is limited to one environment (isolation), we are unable at this point to identify the underlying tone patterns; nevertheless, we can identify that there are two contrastive pitch levels in Mositacha as the examples below illustrate. (152) Phonological contrast in height established in Mositacha [24] ʔaʃo ‘ancestor’ [42] luʃa ‘leg’ [22] koho ‘ram’

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is given. Harlow analyses Mositacha as a restricted tone language (against the 'pitch accent/tone-accent' label): in isolation, disyllabic and trisyllabic nouns show three contrastive surface pitch patterns, HL (most common; H on the first syllable(s), e.g. luʃa [42] 'leg', punita [442] 'coffee'), LH (H on the final syllable, e.g. ʔaʃo [24] 'ancestor', horokʼé [224] 'hippopotamus') and level (no prominent syllable, e.g. koho [22]/[44] 'ram'); the position of the H is lexically unpredictable. Prominence is culminative (at most one prominent syllable per lexical word) but not obligatory (level-pitch words have none). The primary grammar (Wondwosen Tesfaye 2015, not opened) is reported to call the language tone-accent with exactly one high tone per lexical word and no tonal contrast. No true minimal pairs for pitch were found (fn. 20, p. 92).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Verbs: -so verbs are H-falling throughout ([44c]); -eetʃa verbs mostly LHL ([242]), some HL/level; 3sg perfective with he- prefix level (pp. 99-102).
new_statements.exceptions: Level-pitch words lack any prominent syllable (non-obligatory); trisyllabic HL vs level hard to distinguish because final vowels are often voiceless (p. 97). Underlying tones not determined; analysis restricted to isolation forms (§6.2, p. 91).
new_statements.domain_note: Words in isolation (citation forms) only; nouns and verbs treated separately; surface pitch, not underlying tone; data from three speakers of the West (Moro, Toysala) and North (Dubaysho) dialects recorded in Gidole 2012-13.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Harlow 2016 calls the language Mositacha (people: Mosiye; = Bussa [dox], Glottolog buss1239; Wondwosen spells it Mosittacha). Her data are from the West Bussa dialect (Moro, Toysala villages) and the North Bussa dialect (Dubaysho), recorded in Gidole; the third dialect, Nalo, is undescribed. She classifies the language as Konsoid (with Konso, Dirayta) rather than Dullay, contra Ethnologue. No separate glottocodes exist for the dialects.

tone_statements.citation: Balfour, Brittney. 2021. A Brief Grammar of Mositacha Language. Addis Ababa: SIL. 47 pp.
tone_statements.quote: In addition to the segments shown above, tone also plays a major role in Mositacha. Tone is very little studied so far in the language. The marking of tone in this book is not fully consistent and needs to be considered carefully in future publications. ... Also noticeable is the fact that the 1st person and 1st person plural has the same form but has tone variation. ... ፈሊህና I run. ... ፈሊህ̀ና We run. ... However, the first person, singular and plural, habitual and future tense carries the same verb but there is a difference of tone. ... ፍልህነ. I am running ፍልህ̀ነ. I will run ፍልህ́ነ. We will run
tone_statements.locator: p. 10 (end of sec. 1.1 Orthography); p. 28 sec. 6.1 Example 26; p. 29 sec. 6.2 Example 27
tone_statements.summary: Community grammar sketch: tone 'plays a major role', little studied, marked inconsistently (grave/acute on fidel); 1sg vs 1pl and habitual vs future verbs differ only in tone. No inventory or stress.

sources.note: Whole thesis is phonology; ch. 6 'Tone' (pp. 88-104). No stress rule as such: she argues Mositacha is a (restricted) tone language, not pitch accent; reports Wondwosen 2015's 'tone-accent' analysis (one high tone per lexical word, H/L non-contrastive) and disagrees (p. 91). Words in isolation show contrastive pitch patterns HL, LH, level on CVCV nouns (luʃa [42] 'leg', ʔaʃo [24] 'ancestor', koho [22] 'ram'; pp. 91-95) and 442/224/444 on CVCVCV nouns (pp. 96-98); tone culminative but not obligatory. Elsewhere she writes 'word-final, unstressed vowels' (p. 56) without defining stress.
